claims.text: Mildly oxidizing synthesis conditions promote in-situ formation of a thin oxide shell on the nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with an in-situ passivating oxide shell exhibit better high-temperature structural stability than nanoparticles synthesized under inert conditions.
Nanoparticles with an in-situ passivating oxide shell exhibit better high-temperature chemical stability than nanoparticles synthesized under inert conditions.
High oxygen-affinity elements in the nanoparticles selectively form a stable oxide layer during mildly oxidizing synthesis.
The oxide layer acts as a barrier that reduces subsequent oxidation.
The oxide layer slows atomic diffusion during high-temperature operation.
Reduced oxidation and slower atomic diffusion mitigate phase segregation.
Reduced oxidation and slower atomic diffusion mitigate structural degradation.
After high-temperature exposure, oxide-coated nanoparticles will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than inert-synthesized controls.
After high-temperature exposure, oxide-coated nanoparticles will undergo less phase segregation than inert-synthesized controls.
Inert-synthesized nanoparticles without an intentional oxide shell are more prone to oxidation-induced diffusion.
Inert-synthesized nanoparticles without an intentional oxide shell are more prone to phase separation.
The protective mechanism requires a sufficient fraction of high oxygen-affinity elements.
The protective mechanism is expected to operate in moderately oxidizing service environments.
Nanoparticles lacking high oxygen-affinity elements may not receive a protective benefit from mildly oxidizing synthesis.
Strongly oxidizing service conditions may cause excessive oxide growth that eliminates or reverses the protective effect.
